newsitem.title: NORWAY: Size all important for shipping listings - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Size all important for shipping listings - analysts.

text.p: Shipping analysts, split between traditionalists who favour operators staying private and those who see greater opportunities from going public, said on Thursday that size was the real barometer.
Paul Powell, a senior partner at Moore Stephens, said: "I do not think that shipping is good for stock markets or stock markets good for shipping."
"Size is everything in the macho world of stock markets, and most shipping companies simply do not have it," he told the Nor-Shipping '97 conference in Oslo

But Andreas Vergottis, an equity researcher at SBC Warburg, said: "As investor understanding of shipping markets expands, capital markets will acquire a more adventurous stance towards the shipping sector and more capital will increasingly become available at cheaper terms than before."
Deborah Seyman, an analyst at Lazard Capital Markets, agreed that size was important, but said that once achieved, it opens up the doors to benefit from equity markets.
"Consolidation will get companies on the radar screen for equity but size alone will not do that much."
Seyman estimated that a shipping company would need a capital valuation of at least $150 million for even smaller fund managers to take an interest in it.
Powell disagreed: "To get any interest from a stock market, a shipping company needs to have a market capitalisation of over $250 million. Preferably it should be worth at least $500 million."

"Below these levels, fund managers cannot see either the liquidity they need or the size of parcel they want to enable them to take positions which have any influence on their portfolio performance," he added.

But his principal opposition to listing shipping companies rested on factors such as the potentially high cost of raising equity capital, punishing market valuations, the risk of takeover and the difficulty in paying dividends for companies affected by the cyclical nature of shipping markets.

However, Vergottis said: "Shipping is expected to slowly mature in the capital markets. A situation of relative asset price stability provides a healthy environment in which corporate and investor shipping strategy can focus more strongly on creating shareholder value."

Vergottis saw this enhancing long term investment plans rather than the short term approach which in the past has harmed investor goodwill and has prevented shipping share prices from moving at a premium to net asset values.

Seyman also said recent IPOs such as the Knightsbridge Tankers placing proved that the larger shipping issues could succeed and create a stable share price through the required trading liquidity. She said the share price had started at $20 and now risen to around $25.

Vergottis said: "We may foresee that in the not too distant future speculation about the future direction of shipping markets will take place entirely through the use of paper instruments rather than direct investment in steel the ships - though the latter will never disappear altogether."

"Parallel to this, operational control and ownership of steel may consolidate in the hands of few players who will enjoy the efficiencies of large operation and their shares will be priced at premium to NAV," he added. --Reuters Shipping News + 44 171 542 4087. Fax 5107.
